title: The New York Times sues Brave web browser for AI scraping and bypassing paywalls
content:
The New York Times and a group of other publications have filed lawsuits against the company that makes the Brave web browser over alleged unlawful scraping to train AI and also letting users bypass their paywalls, as reported by Reuters.
The New York Times sues Brave web browser for AI scraping and bypassing paywalls
Brave has allegedly provided ‘stolen copyrighted content’ to many AI companies.
According to a complaint filed by the New York Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel, Brave Software has monetized its index of scraped websites by, in part, providing AI companies with paid access to “real-time online content from the Brave Index.” The AI companies then use that index to train their models, access content to “respond to specific user queries,” or both. Brave has allegedly provided “stolen copyrighted content” to “many” AI companies including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere.
Brave also promotes “hundreds of top publishers” as being accessible through its “Paywall blocker” feature in its browser.
“Brave has never asked for the Publishers’ permission to access their websites, much less to copy the material and provide it to users or other AI companies,” the complaint says. “On the contrary, as noted above, Brave allows its users to bypass the Publishers’ paywalls without their consent, and has taken other steps that prevent the Publishers from blocking Brave’s access to the Publishers’ websites. Brave has never compensated the Publishers for the unlawful use, copying, and distribution of the Publishers’ copyrighted content.”
“While we believe in the ethical and responsible use and development of AI, Brave has flouted established copyright law and ignored repeated requests by The Times to stop its infringing conduct,” Graham James, an NYT spokesperson, says in a statement to The Verge. “We filed this lawsuit to hold Brave accountable for stealing our content to power its own products and to provide it to some of the most prominent and well resourced generative AI companies in the world.”
“AI giants are now desperate to avoid getting caught red-handed stealing news from publishers, so Brave Software is selling them a back door to the journalism they know they have no right to,” says Steven Lieberman, the attorney who filed the lawsuit on behalf of the other three publications. “Buying stolen goods secondhand doesn’t make them legitimate. Brave must be held responsible for laundering pirated reporting for the AI industry.”
Brave, Anthropic, Mistral, SpaceXSI, and Cohere didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. “The New York Times is overpaying its attorneys and underpaying its journalists. (Who could’ve easily identified the disinformation in this suit.)” says Jesse Dwyer, Perplexity’s chief communications officer.
Update, November 2nd: Clarified that one lawsuit was filed by New York Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel, not the companies that run them. Also added a statement from the attorney who filed the lawsuit on behalf of those publications.

report.summary: The New York Times and other newspapers sued Brave, alleging it scraped paywalled news, sold access to AI firms, and helped users bypass paywalls.
report.background: The lawsuit lands amid growing tension between publishers and AI companies over how copyrighted news is used to train models and answer real-time queries. Publishers rely on subscriptions and paywalls, while AI firms seek fresh, comprehensive web data. Search engines and browser makers sit in the middle because their indexes can feed AI systems directly. The New York Times has already sued OpenAI and Microsoft over AI training, and other news organizations are pursuing licensing deals or litigation. Brave operates its own browser and search index, and it markets privacy-focused tools, including a paywall-bypassing feature. The case tests whether an intermediary that supplies scraped content to AI companies can be held liable alongside those AI companies.
key_points: The New York Times filed suit against Brave Software, while the New York Daily News, Chicago Tribune, and Orlando Sentinel filed a separate complaint. The publishers allege Brave scraped their sites without permission, copied copyrighted material, and distributed it to users and AI companies without compensation.

The complaints allege Brave monetizes its index by selling AI companies paid access to real-time content from the Brave Index. Those companies allegedly use the content to train models, answer user queries, or both. The suit names Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere as recipients of allegedly stolen copyrighted content.

Brave promotes a paywall blocker that it says works with hundreds of top publishers, according to the complaint. The publishers say Brave lets users bypass paywalls without consent and takes steps that stop publishers from blocking Brave’s access. They argue Brave never asked permission or paid for the use.

The Times says Brave ignored repeated requests to stop infringing conduct and flouted copyright law. The plaintiffs’ attorney accuses Brave of selling AI companies a “back door” to journalism and “laundering pirated reporting.” Brave and several named AI companies did not immediately comment; Perplexity’s communications chief dismissed the suit.

The dispute highlights how AI training and real-time answer systems depend on web indexes and scraped content. It also raises questions about browser features that alter paywalls and about whether index providers can be liable for content they supply to AI developers.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the case threatens a less visible part of the data supply chain: intermediaries that package web indexes for model training and retrieval. If courts accept the publishers’ theory, AI companies may need stronger provenance checks and licensing agreements not just with crawlers but with search and browser data providers. Developers using search APIs, crawler feeds, or retrieval-augmented generation pipelines should expect more contractual and technical scrutiny of content rights. For regular users, paywall-bypass features could face legal or product changes, and publishers may tighten blocking. The lawsuit does not yet establish liability, but it signals that copyright fights are expanding from model makers to data brokers and browser companies.
report.tools: Watch Brave Search API and Brave’s paywall-blocker feature as the services central to the allegations. Publishers and developers can follow robots.txt and the open-source ai.robots.txt project, Cloudflare’s AI crawler controls, and bot-management logs to track AI scraping. For compliance, audit data-source licenses and publisher opt-outs before feeding indexed web content into AI training or retrieval systems.
